# Understanding the Role of Adipocytes and Fibroblasts in Cancer

**Authors:** Mauricio A. Downer; Michelle F. Griffin; Annah G. Morgan; Jennifer B. Parker; Dayan J. Li; Charlotte E Berry; Norah E. Liang; Lionel Kameni; Asha C. Cotterell; Deena Akras; Caleb Valencia; Michael T. Longaker; Derrick C. Wan

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Surgery, Division of Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA 94305, USA | 2Institute for Stem Cell Biology and Regenerative Medicine, Stanford University School of Medicine, Stanford, CA 94305, USA

## Abstract

Cancer is currently the second leading cause of death in the United States. There is increasing evidence that the tumor microenvironment (TME) is pivotal for tumorigenesis and metastasis. Recently, adipocytes and cancer associated fibroblast (CAFs) in the TME have been shown to play a major role in tumorigenesis of different cancers, specifically melanoma. Animal studies have shown that CAFs and adipocytes within the TME help tumors evade the immune system, for example, by releasing chemokines to blunt the effectiveness of the host defense. Though studies have identified that adipocytes and CAFs play a role in tumorigenesis, adipocyte transition to fibroblast within the TME is fairly unknown. This review intends to elucidate the potential adipocytes may have to transition to fibroblasts, and as part of the TME, a critical role CAFS may play in affecting the growth and invasion of tumor cells. Future studies that illuminate the function of adipocytes and CAFs in the TME may pave way for new anti-tumor therapies.

## Introduction

Cancer is currently the second most common cause of death in the United States.1 In the year 2020, there were an estimated 19.3 million new cancer cases worldwide, and nearly 10 million cancer deaths.2 Despite the development of innovative therapies, cancers such as malignant melanoma still led to significant morbidity and mortality.3 Both environmental factors and genetics impact tumorigenesis and cancer prognosis, but the extent to which they play a role in carcinogenesis is still an area of active investigation.4 Recently, adipocytes and fibroblasts within the tumor microenvironment (TME) have garnered interest due to their plasticity and function in modulating tumor growth.3,5

Fibroblasts are mesenchymal cells that actively participate in tissue homeostasis and disease by producing extracellular matrix (ECM) and signal with immune cells.3 Fibroblasts are primarily believed to be important in tissue repair due to their plasticity, but this feature may contribute to disease.3Adipocytes also display plasticity, which may similarly facilitate cancer proliferation.3,5

Recently, fibroblast and adipocyte function has been linked to tumorigenesis and progression of metastases.5 Studies suggest that obese patients do not respond well to cancer treatment because of the increased adipose tissue.6 Adipocytes and fibroblasts within the proximity of the tumor may secrete adipokines and cytokines, which are known to promote tumor development.5,6 In light of these emerging findings, this review aims to: 1) describe the role of cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and adipocytes in tumorigenesis and 2) detail the malignant potential of melanoma due to increased adipocyte deposition.

## Tumorigenesis and tumor microenvironment

A tumor is the abnormal growth of cells due to genetic and epigenetic alterations.7 It encompasses both the cancer cells and the surrounding milieu composed of a varying collection of infiltrating and local host cells, secreted factors, and ECM.7 Tumor cells activate molecular, cellular, and physical changes within host tissues to support tumor growth and progression.8 These alterations to host tissue constitute what scientists call the (TME) (Figure 1).8 The TME includes CAFs, immune cells, adipocytes, a varying degree of stromal cells, blood vessels, and ECM.7,8,9

## Cancer-associated fibroblast definition

CAFs are activated fibroblasts believed to be associated with a poor prognosis in cancer patients.8,9 Currently, there is no universally accepted definition of a CAF.8 However, they do express higher levels of alpha smooth muscle actin (α-SMA) compared to fibroblasts.8 ⍺-SMA is an actin isoform that is most prominent in vascular smooth muscle cells8, and may play an important role in skin fibrosis through myofibroblast activity.10 Notably higher amounts of α-SMA in CAFs have been linked to chemotherapeutic resistance for patients due to the increased fibrosis.8 Studies have also shown that CAFs have many more biomarkers that help distinguish them from normal fibroblasts.11 These include fibroblast specific protein-1, also known as S100A4, fibroblast-activating protein, platelet derived growth receptor alpha/beta, tenascin-C, desmin, collagen 1-α1, vimentin, and fibronectin.11

## Role of CAFs in cancer

CAFs have been described in many different malignancies such as breast cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and melanoma.7,8,11,12,13 CAFs play several roles in tumor development. Within the tumor microenvironment, CAFs secrete exosomes, growth factors, inflammatory ligands, and ECM proteins that promote cancer cell proliferation, therapy resistance, and immune evasiveness.12

A major factor linking CAFs to cancer proliferation is the abundant release of different chemokines and cytokines throughout the tumor microenvironment.11,13 Chemokines are known to regulate the recruitment of inflammatory cells.11,13 Cytokines encompass a diverse collection of pro-and anti-inflammatory molecules that are categorized based on the structural similarity of their receptors.14 Among these cytokines are chemokines that constitute a subset of secreted proteins with the specific function of initiating cellular migration.14 These cytokines and chemokines present within the tumor microenvironment increase cancer proliferation and malignancy.11,13

Chemokines, such as C-C motif ligand-2 (CCL-2) produced by CAFs, stimulate cancer stem cell self-renewal in breast cancer.11,13 Similarly CCL-5 has been shown to promote tumorigenesis.11,13 In mice, CCL-5 released by CAFs has been linked to the proliferation and invasion of ovarian cancer cells.11,13 Furthermore, Papaccio et al. showed that CAFs may release chemokines such as chemokine receptor type 4/ chemokine receptor type 5(CXCR4/CXCR5).11 These chemokines are known to be upregulated in other cancers such as melanoma and hepatocellular carcinoma.11,13 Cytokines released from CAFs include Interleukin (IL)-6, transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).15,16 IL-6 acts as a chemotactic for macrophages to access the TME, which may aid in cancer proliferation by supporting angiogenesis within the tumor while VEGF and TGF-β may downregulate immune cells necessary for tumor suppression.11,13,15,17,18 Foster et al. provided an integrated analysis of CAFs subpopulations, which identified three superclusters of CAFs.19 The three superclusters were identified as steady state, mechanoresponsive, and immunomodulatory CAFs. Disruption of underlying mechanical forces or immune checkpoint inhibition therapy led to a shift of CAFs to different subpopulations and consequently affected tumor growth.19 The manipulation of CAFs may be another route to decreasing tumor proliferation.

CAFs have the ability to downregulate the immune system along with being pro- inflammatory.20 Li et al. showed that in mice both programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) and α-SMA were upregulated due to increased CAFs in the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) of both melanoma and colorectal cancer.20 The TIME is a component of the TME which may upregulate or downregulate immune receptors based on the needs of the tumor, highlighting the complex role of CAFs in both immune activation and suppression within the TME.20 Increased levels of PD-L1 in the TIME aids in tumor immune escape, while α-SMA may increase fibrosis within the TIME.20

## Tumor immune microenvironment

TIME has been linked to the clinical prognosis of patients with tumors.21 It is made up of immune cell populations within the TME, which include innate and adaptive immune cells such as myeloid cells and lymphocytes.21 These immune cells in the TIME may release cytokines such as IL-1β, which may be responsible for the conversion of fibroblasts into pro-inflammatory CAFs.21

Cytokines released from the TIME are currently a topic of interest for cancer research. In mice, it was shown that the upregulation of IL-33 played a major factor in the metastasis of breast cancer to the lungs.22 Upregulation of IL-33 in mice increased metastases by recruiting different immune cells to the TIME and targeting IL-33 inhibited breast cancer metastasis to the lungs.22 Overall, evidence suggests that the TIME plays an important role in tumorigenesis.

## Types of Adipose Tissue

Adipose tissue can be largely found in two compartments, the visceral layer and the subcutaneous layer of the body. Visceral fat is the fat found around the organs.23 An increase in visceral fat has been linked to liver disease, cardiometabolic disease, and type 2 diabetes.23 Subcutaneous fat is considered to be the largest fat depot of adipose tissue, and is largely responsible for inflammation and insulin resistance.24 Studies have shown that age equivalent obese mice were more susceptible to tumor angiogenesis and breast tumor growth secondary to greater subcutaneous fat and the role this may play in promoting inflammation, with increased expression of inflammatory markers such as VEGF.25 It is also believed that subcutaneous fat may be important for the progression of certain skin cancers like squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma.26,27

## The role of adipocytes and stromal cells in the TME

Fat within the body is comprised of a heterogenous cell population consisting of adipocytes and stromal vascular cells.28 Park et al. demonstrated that adipocytes and cells within the stromal vascular fraction may contribute to tumor proliferation.28 As tumors grow within an adipose-rich TME, adipocytes may function as endocrine cells to shape the TME.28 Adipocytes may release signaling molecules such as adipokines and extracellular matrix constitutents.28 When tumor cells begin to proliferate within the adipose-rich environment, adipose tissue may start to grow as well. As the adipose tissue expands, this may lead to tissue hypoxia and compensatory angiogenesis.28 Hypoxia may also cause adipocytes to release hypoxia inducible factor-1 alpha (HIF-1⍺) and proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, tumor necrosis factor, IL-1β and CCL-2.28 HIF-1⍺ upregulates profibrotic pathways involved in matrix proteins and the proinflammatory cytokines aforementioned have been directly implicated in tumor metastasis, growth, and poor prognosis.28

The stromal vascular fraction within the adipose rich TME may similarly undergo rapid expansion as the tumor grows.28 Adipocyte progenitor cells both proliferate and differentiate into mature adipocytes.28 Park et al. reported that these adipocyte progenitor cells were key for the survival of the tumor in the TME and referred to them as cancer associated adipocytes (CAAs).28 Their study in obese patients showed that an increase in CAAs contributed to tumor progression through formation of endothelial precursors, pericytes, and adipocytes, which result in increased angiogenesis and cancer cell proliferation.28

## CAA within the TME source

CAAs within the TME are important for cancer growth and metastasis. As the tumor grows, CAAs may also undergo a functional change within the TME, leading to loss of adipogenic markers and an increase in a fibroblast-like phenotypes.28 CAAs also release cytokines and free fatty acids to support drug evasiveness and aggression of the tumor. Cancer cells, CAFs, and CAAs are able to communicate through proinflammatory cytokines to maintain the environment necessary for tumor survival.28,29,30,31 (Figure 2). The crosstalk between tumor cells, CAFs, and CAAs has been suggested to be necessary for the survival and proliferation of breast cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and more recently melanoma.26,28,29,30,31

## CAFs in Melanoma

Melanoma is an aggressive neoplasm responsible for 1–2 % of all cancer deaths in the United States.11 Uncertainties regarding the role CAFs play in melanoma have led to increased investigation regarding how they may affect tumor staging.11 Papaccio et al. performed a melanoma study illustrating that CAFs were important for melanoma invasiveness.11 This study found that release of cytokines like IL-6 from CAFs, was important for melanoma growth and invasion.11 Although the study had limitations defining the composition of melanoma CAFs, they showed that there may be a correlation between the number of CAFs within a melanoma and poor prognosis.11

## Animal studies on CAFs and melanoma

Animal studies show promising results in melanoma treatment when targeting CAFs and the their cytokines.20 Current research shows a correlation between the quantity of CAFs found in the TME and the ability for melanoma, colorectal cancer, and esophageal cancer to evade the immune system.20 Li et al. highlighted the role of CAFs in melanoma, concluding that there may be a correlation between CAFs and the release of PD-L1 in mice.20 This study found that C-X-C motif chemokines (CXCL) 5 is among the most abundant cytokines released from CAFs, and that blocking CXCL5 decreased the expression of PD-L1.20 This may point to a novel strategy of treating melanoma in the future.

## Adipocytes and CAA effects on melanoma

CAAs, like CAFs have been a target of drug therapy for many different types of cancer, including melanoma.31 Current therapies for melanoma generally do not target adipocytes but include immunotherapies through the inhibition of cellular signaling genes such as B-Raf proto-oncogne serine/threonine kinase and mitogen activated protein kinase which have shown promise in suppressing cell growth and proliferation of melanoma.32 Other melanoma immunotherapies include inhibiting cytotoxic T lymphocyte associated antigen-4 and PD-L1 to increase immune response against the cancer.33 Though immunotherapies against melanoma have been successful, it is generally unknown how immunotherapies affect adipocytes within the TME.

A study by Zoico and colleagues on obesity in mice observed that melanoma increased in aggression with increasing amounts of adipose tissue within the vicinity of the tumor.31 They also observed the transition of peritumoral adipocytes into proinflammatory adipocytes, evocatively like CAAs, and then into fibroblast-like cells, that not only lost their adipocyte-like properties, but also began to express increased collagen andmetalloproteinases.31

Adipocyte to fibroblast transition is a mechanism by which adipocytes may play a role in tumorigenesis.5 As a cancer progresses, the tumor encounters adipocytes and can induce changes in their morphology.5 While the adipocyte may remain an adipocyte at first, decreased lipid content and adipocyte marker expression has been observed.5 Bochet et al. found that adipocytes may de-differentiate into a CAA which release cytokines and free fatty acid to maintain the TME. Furthermore, they may begin to produce more ECM proteins.5,28 With increased expression of ECM components, CAAs become less adipocyte like and phenotypically mirror fibroblasts instead.5,28 The adipocyte-derived-fibroblasts continue to release cytokines and proteases, which can increase aggressiveness of the melanoma.5,28 Though the origin of CAFs is unclear, Bochet et al. believe that the transition of adipocytes to CAAs and eventually to fibroblasts may significantly contribute to CAF production.5

## Anti-adipogenic drugs for melanoma

While melanomas can have aggressive behavior, if caught early, they can be treated with surgical excision alone with high survival rates.34 When melanoma goes unnoticed and has a chance to metastasize, survival rate drops significantly.34 Early detection is thus key for survival; misdiagnosis of melanoma can be devastating as the patient would miss the window for surgical excision.34

Once melanoma metastasizes from the skin to distant organs, the median survival rate in patients drops to about 6 months.35 Recent studies suggest that once melanoma invades the subcutaneous fat, the tumor aggressiveness increases.11 Therefore, researchers have begun to target adipocytes as a novel way to combat the invasiveness of the melanoma.36,37 Drugs that decrease the amount of adipose tissue within the TME may be able to impair formation of CAAs and the transition into an adipocyte-derived fibroblast.5 The use of anti-adipogenic drugs such as metformin and thiazolidinediones (TZD) - Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) gamma agonists - has shown promise in slowing down the spread of a degree of cancers such as melanoma. The utilization of anti-diabetic treatment presents a potentially valuable approach for the treatment of melanoma, as well as various other types of cancers.36,37,38–40,41–47

## Metformin use for melanoma treatment

Animal studies have shown that decreasing the adipocyte density within the TME may lead to better therapy responsiveness and may decrease the metastatic potential of melanoma.36 High-fat diet animal models have been found to increase progression of melanoma, whereas in animals fed a low fat diet or with increased exercise, melanoma progression was hampered.48 There is also extensive research on the use of various anti-diabetic drugs with cancer, which have reported decreased drug resistance of different tumors.36,37,48,49 Metformin has been used against a plethora of tumors (colon cancer, breast cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma), with mixed evidence on its effectiveness against cancers.36

Metformin works by exerting anti-hyperglycemic effects, which suppresses hepatic glucose through AMPK-dependent and independent pathways.36 Metformin may also decrease fat accumulation by increasing expression of fibroblast growth factor 21, a protein that promotes lipolysis in adipose tissue.36 These effects on plasma glucose levels and adipocyte function may work in concert to decrease drug resistance and metastatic ability of melanoma as shown in mouse studies.36 However, more investigation is needed on the use of metformin as an anti-adipogenic drug for melanoma.

## Pioglitazone Use for Melanoma Treatment

Pioglitazone is a TZD that functions as a synthetic ligand for peroxisome proliferator activated receptors which alter the transcription of genes responsible for carbohydrate and lipid metabolism.50 This may result in improved glycemic control insulin sensitivity.50 Pioglitazone has shown some promise in inhibiting tumorigenesis in melanoma through the upregulation of peroxisome proliferator activated receptors.51 Dana et al. conducted a study demonstrating that the PPARgamma agonist may have a beneficial effect against melanoma via interfering with the toll like receptor 4 (TLR4)-dependent signaling pathway.51 Cuesta et al. revealed that TLR4 is expressed by immune cells and adipocytes, and the inhibition of TLR4 decreased both adipogenesis and inflammatory immune response.52

However, there is currently much debate on how effective TZDs are on melanoma, with conflicting reports of the drugs being anti-proliferative or pro-proliferative.37,53 A recent study found that pioglitazone may be effective due to its anti-inflammatory response and agonistic effect on PPARgamma.37,53 Although preliminary results are promising, the mechanism of action as it relates to the adipocytes, fibroblasts, and immune system of the TME is still largely unknown.37,49

## Future Studies

Future studies are needed to explore the role that adipocytes and fibroblasts play in cancers such as melanoma. With better understanding, drugs such as pioglitazone may be useful in melanoma. Today, only a few small animal studies have been performed following adipocyte and CAF progression with melanoma. More studies are thus needed to investigate whether a decrease in adipocytes may reduce inflammatory markers within the TME, potentially slowing the progression of melanoma.

## Conclusion

Increasing evidence to date show that adipocytes and CAFs could play a major role in tumorigenesis in cancers, including melanoma. Future studies exploring the potential role of antidiabetic drugs as tumor inhibitors may highlight new and more effective approaches in cancer therapy.

## Abstract

Background: Surgical intervention for spontaneous pneumothorax typically includes mechanical

pleurodesis that frequently utilizes a bovie scratch pad given its universal presence, low cost and ease of

use. The pad is folded on itself after dividing it in half, allowing easier passage through the smaller

incisions. This case is reported to raise awareness that dividing the scratch pad may allow the embedded

radio-opaque marker to fall out and become retained as a foreign body.

Case presentation: The patient is a 41 year-old female who presented with shortness of breath secondary

to spontaneous pneumothorax. Chest CT scan showed apical blebs. The patient underwent video assisted thorascopic surgery (VATS) with bleb resection and mechanical pleurodesis using a divided and

folded bovie scratch pad. Postoperative chest x-ray showed a retained foreign body. Reoperation

confirmed this to be the radio-opaque marker of the scratch pad and was removed. The patient did well

and was discharge the following day.

Conclusion: Dividing the bovie scratch pad may damage and “weaken” the product allowing the radio-

opaque marker to fall out during its use for pleurodesis and should be discouraged.  Recommendation is

made of using the scratch pad as a whole and not dividing it.

## Background

Spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs among tall thin adolescent men with an annual incidence of

18-28 and 1.2-6 cases per 100,000 men and women, respectively.1

It may follow activities that increase intrathoracic pressure but can also occur at rest. Symptoms often

include chest pain and/or acute dyspnea, and may resolve spontaneously within 24-hours with no

intervention.2 Medical management includes observation for first time smaller pneumothoraces,

especially if patients are minimally symptomatic. Tube thoracostomy is usually required in symptomatic patients with larger pneumothoraces.

Video assisted thorascopic surgery (VATS) is performed in cases of recurrences and when blebs are identified radiographically. Surgery usually includes bleb resection in addition to mechanical pleurodesis

aimed at promoting adhesions that would prevent lung collapse in case of a recurrence.

It was customary for us to fold the scratch pad on itself after dividing it in half in order to pass it through the smaller VATS incisions. This case is reported to raise awareness that such practice of dividing the

scratch pad may damage and weaken the product, allowing the radio-opaque marker to easily separate during its actual use while performing the pleurodesis and become a retrained foreign body. Informed consent was obtained from the patient. Institutional review board approval was not required and was

waived for the purpose of this study.

## Case Presentation

The patient is a 41 year-old female who presented with acute shortness of breath. Chest x-ray and computed tomography showed spontaneous pneumothorax with apical blebs.  The patient underwent

uneventful Video Assisted Thorascopic Surgery (VATS) with bleb resection and mechanical pleurodesis. Half of a folded Bovie scratch pad that is usually used as a cautery tip cleaner (CardinalHealth, fig.1) was

utilized to abrade the parietal pleura. The postoperative portable chest x-ray reported no unusual findings (fig.2). Following chest tube removal, on postop day-3 prior to discharge, a two-view chest x-ray showed

an apical pneumothorax, in addition to an “abnormality” in the apex of the hemithorax (fig.3) consistent with a foreign body (FB). Options, including no intervention versus VATS retrieval of the FB, were discussed with the patient who opted for the latter. Intraoperatively, the FB was easily identified and

removed (fig.4). The patient was discharged the following day in good condition. The FB was confirmed to be the radio-opaque marker of the Bovie scratch pad.

## Discussion

Surgical intervention for spontaneous pneumothorax is recommended for blebs identified on chest CTscans, especially in cases of recurrence or in patients who might engage in “high-risk situations”, such as

flying, scuba diving or hiking, where access to medical care may not be immediately available. Surgery is typically performed through VATS approach that includes bleb resection and pleurodesis, usually

mechanical, aimed at preventing lung collapse and tension pneumothorax in case of a recurrence by

creating adhesions between the parietal and visceral pleura.3,4

Mechanical pleurodesis is frequently accomplished by using the Bovie scratch pad, an off-label application (fig.1).  It is intended to clean the electro-cautery tip when needed; however, its universal

presence, low cost and ease of use have led many thoracic surgeons to use them for pleurodesis. Its use has been reported by others and described in the training manual of the Society of Thoracic Surgery

(STS).5 We have successfully carried out this practice for many years without any adverse effects.

The instrument count at the conclusion of the operation was correct, as the counted item was the pad itself and not the marker. The radiological report of the immediate portable postop chest x-ray did not

mention the FB, although in retrospect it can be visualized. The marker was in close proximity to the parenchymal staple line and thought to be part of it (fig.2). It became more apparent when an apical

pneumothorax, following chest tube removal on day three, moved the staple line away from the marker (fig.3). Our index of suspicion was high that the abnormality seen was the marker but could not be

absolutely certain, as the pad had been already discarded as one might expect.

It was formerly customary for us to cut the scratch pad in half for easier introduction through the small VATS incision. This perhaps “weakened” the product and permitted the marker to separate from the pad, as it is difficult to remove it from an intact and uncut pad. One thought was to remove the marker off the cut pad prior to its insertion into the chest. This perhaps may create a worse problem of retaining an

unmarked pad that cannot be detected radiographically in case of an incorrect count. It is also against

devices.

Our current practice is to use a full (uncut) folded pad and continue to perform pleurodesis per STS guidelines, unless further studies corroborate the work by Min et al. showing no difference in recurrence

rates in patients with and without pleurodesis.6 A conscious effort is also made at the end of each case to specifically identify the marker within the scratch pad at time of instrument count.

Abstract

Background: Surgical intervention for spontaneous pneumothorax typically includes mechanical pleurodesis that frequently utilizes a Bovie scratch pad given its universal presence, low cost and ease of use. The pad is folded on itself after dividing it in half, allowing easier passage through the smaller incisions. However, unintentional foreign body retention may occur during the course of an operation leading to reoperations or even worse complications. This case is reported to raise awareness that dividing the scratch pad may allow the embedded radio-opaque marker to fall out and become retained as a foreign body. Postoperative chest x-ray showed a retained foreign body. Reoperation confirmed this to be the radio-opaque marker of the scratch pad and was removed. The patient did well and was discharged the following day. Conclusion: Dividing the bovie scratch pad may damage and “weaken” the product allowing the radio- opaque marker to fall out during its use for pleurodesis and should be discouraged. Recommendation is made of using the scratch pad as a whole and not dividing it.

# CASE REPORT

Transfemoral aortic valve replacement in a nonagenarian with aortic stenosis and cardiac amyloidosis: case report

Deena Akras1, Keith Bullinger2, Meera Kondapaneni2, Aisha Siraj1,2, Rami Akhrass1,2*   and Ashish Aneja2

Abstract Background:  Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is diagnosed with increasing frequency in the elderly population with severe aortic stenosis (AS), especially with the low-flow, low- gradient phenotype. Prognosis is poor with no treatment. Case presentation:  The patient is a 94-year-old active male who presented with a stroke that fully resolved. He was found to have low-flow, low-gradient severe AS, along with concomitant CA. Gradients across the aortic valve worsened with the dobutamine challenge test. He underwent successful transfemoral aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and did well postoperatively, where he remained in the hospital for only one day. Treatment of his CA with Tafamidis was recommended; however, the patient declined due to its cost and personal preference. Conclusion:  To our knowledge, we report on one of the oldest patients to undergo TAVR for low-flow, low-gradient AS with concurrent CA (AS-CA). It might be prudent to screen elderly patients with AS for CA, as prognosis is worse with medical management alone. TAVR has overall improved survival in patients with AS-CA and is considered the procedure of choice, as these patients are typically older and at higher risk for surgical intervention.

Introduction Aortic stenosis (AS) is the most common valvular heart disease, with a prevalence of 4% in patients older than 80  years of age. Cardiac amyloidosis (CA), manifested by extracellular deposit of amyloid fibrils within the myocardium and other structures, affects up to 25% of octogenarians. CA has been increasingly detected and diagnosed due to advances in cardiac imaging, and is reportedly associated with a threefold increase in mortality in patients with AS when left untreated [1, 2]. It is estimated that 15% of patients with AS and up to 30% of the subset with low-flow, low-gradient AS may have concomitant CA, which increases the risk of heart

failure and mortality [2]. AS with CA (AS-CA) is associated with significantly worse outcomes for patients who undergo medical management alone, with a reported one-year mortality of 54% compared to 31% for isolated AS. However, with aortic valve replacement (AVR), mortality improves to 16% for AS-CA compared with 10% for isolated AS [3]. Transfemoral aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has become the procedure of choice for severe AS in the elderly who are at higher risk with surgical AVR (SAVR), and its use has steadily expanded to include patients in lower risk groups as well [4]. It has been shown to improve survival compared with medical management in patients with AS associated with CA [3]. We report on one of the oldest patients to our knowledge who underwent TAVR for low-flow, low-gradient severe AS with associated CA. Informed consent was obtained from the patient. Case report The patient is a 94-year-old active male with a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia and stage 3A renal insufficiency, who presented to the emergency department with mental status changes, in addition to months-long worsening of exertional dyspnea. He was diagnosed with a stroke with findings on head computed tomography of a hypodense area in the right occipital region, most likely due to new-onset atrial fibrillation (AF). Echocardiography showed concentric left ventricular wall thickening with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 40%, in addition to evidence of severe AS with aortic valve (AV) area of 0.8 ­cm2 and peak and mean gradients of 29 mmHg and 18 mmHg, respectively. Heart catheterization demonstrated mild coronary artery disease as well as low-flow, low-gradient severe AS. Baseline mean AV gradient was 18 mmHg with a valve area of 0.6 ­cm2 and transvalvular flow rate of 112.18 mL/ sec. Dobutamine challenge at 10 mcg/kg/min revealed an increase in mean AV gradient to 47 mmHg and valve area of 0.8 ­cm2. The transvalvular flow rate more than doubled to 243.45 mL/s, confirming severe AS. The patient’s electrocardiogram (Fig. 1) did not show signs of left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), raising suspicion for CA. Nuclear scintigraphy with technetium pyrophosphate was highly

consistent with wild-type (transthyretin) cardiac amyloidosis (Fig. 2). The patient was placed on aspirin (ASA) and direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) for his AF and stroke. His neurological symptoms completely resolved at the time of his initial presentation, and he underwent successful TAVR two months later (Fig. 3). Postoperatively, the patient was observed in the intensive care unit and was discharged home the following day with no complications. His anticoagulants (ASA and DOAC) were continued, and follow-up echocardiography demonstrated normal functioning of the prosthetic valve with AV area of 2.0 ­cm2 and peak and mean gradients of 9 mmHg and 5 mmHg, respectively. Treatment of his CA with Tafamidis was recommended; however, the patient declined due to its cost and personal preference.

Discussion AS and CA are more prevalent in older patients. However, age alone does not explain their frequent concurrence, as the prevalence of CA in the general population older than 80  years of age is only 1% compared with 8–16% observed in patients with AS [5, 6]. CA is a progressive infiltrative cardiomyopathy in which deposits of amyloid, either immunoglobulin light-chain (AL) or transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), accumulate in the myocardium. ATTR is usually acquired and of the wildtype, formerly known as senile amyloidosis [7]. ATTR

cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR-CA) is the most common cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy in the elderly, and diagnosis is frequently delayed until later stages, when symptoms of heart failure appear. The median survival in untreated patients from the time of diagnosis is around 25–41 months, with longer survival in patients with wildtype CA [6]. AS associated with CA has worse clinical presentation and portends a worse prognosis unless treated [3, 7]. A clinical scoring system (RAISE) has been developed to screen patients with AS for concomitant CA, including: cardiac Remodeling (left ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction), Age, cardiac Injury (high-sensitivity troponin T, Systemic disease (carpel tunnel syndrome) and Electrical disturbances (right bundle branch block, low voltage). Such patients should receive further testing with cardiac imaging and free light chain assessment [5]. In patients with symptomatic severe low-flow, lowgradient AS with reduced LVEF, the American College of Cardiology recommends echocardiographic measurements with low-dose dobutamine stress testing if certain criteria on the patient’s baseline echocardiogram are met. These consist of a calcified aortic valve with reduced systolic opening, LVEF less than 50%, calculated valve area 1.0 ­cm2 or less, and aortic velocity less than 4.0 m/s or mean gradient less than 40  mmHg. Severe AS is confirmed if the transvalvular velocity reaches 4.0 m/s with a valve area less than 1.0 ­cm2 during low-dose dobutamine

infusion up to a maximum of 20 mcg/kg/min. Stress testing also helps to identify whether or not significant contractile reserve is present. Patients who do not show an increase in stroke volume of at least 20% in response to dobutamine carry a poor prognosis [8]. Unique in our patient is his preservation of contractile reserve, where his aortic transvalvular flow rate more than doubled during a dobutamine 10-mcg/kg/min challenge exam. The introduction of more effective treatments for ATTR amyloidosis promises to reduce the post-TAVR mortality further in this high-risk group. Chemotherapy directed toward plasma cell dyscrasias in AL amyloidosis can be effective. Tafamidis, a transthyretin-stabilizing benzoxazole derivative, has been shown to reduce mortality [9]. Other medications, known as ATTR silencers, have been approved for the treatment of ATTR associated with neuropathy. These drugs act through RNA interference mechanisms and show promise in preventing myocardial seeding with ATTR as well as chain formation. Investigation into ATTR-CA is rapidly changing the accepted paradigm of a progressive and terminal disease to one that is becoming ever more treatable. The prevalence of ATTR-CA in patients undergoing TAVR is 8–16%. The presence of ATTR-CA in patients undergoing TAVR was found not to affect post-TAVR mortality; however, an increase in post-TAVR heart failure hospitalizations has been reported and is thought to be secondary to underlying infiltrative cardiomyopathy [6]. Given the high prevalence of AS and increasing frequency of TAVR procedures, it might be prudent to screen patients in whom there is suspicion of associated ATTR-CA, as management and prognosis differ from other cardiomyopathies [10].

Conclusion To our knowledge, we report on one of the oldest patients to undergo TAVR for low-flow, low-gradient severe AS associated with CA. The fact that our patient retained significant contractile reserve and achieved an aortic transvalvular flow rate of nearly 250 mL/s is noteworthy. Elderly patients with AS commonly have concomitant CA and further pharmacological challenge testing might be advisable, especially when other associated features are present. Medical treatment alone for AS-CA carries a poor prognosis and valve replacement should be strongly considered. TAVR is advised over SAVR, as these patients are typically older and at higher surgical risk.
